title: Training & Canopy Management
learningOutcome: Understand canopy training as a controlled change to plant architecture, light interception, mechanical loading, airflow and access; choose techniques from plant vigor and crop goals; and evaluate topping, bending, pruning, trellising and support by measured recovery and canopy performance rather than technique folklore.
evidenceNote: Training changes geometry and tissue allocation; it does not create energy or guarantee yield. Compare architecture, light distribution, environmental uniformity, labor, recovery and final crop outcomes under the actual cultivar and production system.

chapters.title: Architecture, Meristems & Training Goals
chapters.objective: Connect meristem biology, apical dominance, stem growth and crop objectives before selecting a training technique.

lessons.title: Meristems define the plant's available growth points
lessons.summary: Shoot and axillary meristems create new stems, leaves and branches; training changes which of those growth points continue, compete or become exposed.
lessons.cultivation: Map active tips before cutting or bending so the intervention matches the desired final architecture.
lessons.observe: Record node number, active growth points, branch order, plant height and developmental stage before intervention.

lessons.title: Apical dominance is a network, not one hormone switch
lessons.summary: Auxin, sugars, cytokinins, strigolactones, bud maturity, light and root resources interact in branch release after the main apex is bent or removed.
lessons.cultivation: Do not assume every topped plant will release the same number or strength of branches.
lessons.observe: Track which buds break, days to visible growth, branch length, symmetry and plant vigor after treatment.

lessons.title: Primary growth and stem thickening solve different problems
lessons.summary: Length growth expands canopy reach while secondary thickening increases transport and mechanical capacity of established axes.
lessons.cultivation: Fast elongation can create long lever arms before stems and branch attachments are ready for later load.
lessons.observe: Measure height, internode length, stem diameter, branch angle and support requirement over time.

lessons.title: Define the crop objective before choosing the technique
lessons.summary: A useful training objective can be lower height, more uniform light, better access, improved support, reduced density or a controlled branch count; technique names are not objectives.
lessons.cultivation: Choose the smallest intervention that addresses the measured architectural problem.
lessons.observe: Write the target outcome, available footprint, headroom, labor/access constraints and acceptance criteria before treatment.

knowledgeChecks: What is an axillary meristem?
Why does topping not produce identical branch release in every plant?
How does stem thickening differ from shoot elongation?
What makes a training goal measurable?

chapters.title: Low-Stress Bending, Positioning & Ties
chapters.objective: Use gradual positioning to change canopy geometry while protecting vascular continuity and allowing for stem growth.

lessons.title: Bending changes position without removing the apex
lessons.summary: Repositioning a shoot can reduce positional dominance, expose other growth points and redistribute the canopy without the tissue loss of topping.
lessons.cultivation: Use gradual changes when the objective can be achieved by geometry rather than tissue removal.
lessons.observe: Record bend location, angle, branch flexibility, leaf posture and growth-point response.

lessons.title: Stem age and bend radius change injury risk
lessons.summary: Young flexible tissue tolerates curvature differently from older lignified stems; sharp kinks concentrate strain and can damage vascular tissues.
lessons.cultivation: Avoid forcing a branch beyond the mechanical range needed for the canopy objective.
lessons.observe: Check for creasing, collapse, discoloration, loss of turgor and recovery distal to the bend.

lessons.title: Ties and clips become hazards as stems expand
lessons.summary: A support that is loose at installation can later constrict a growing stem, abrade tissue or create a weak loading point.
lessons.cultivation: Use adjustable attachments and inspect them throughout stem expansion.
lessons.observe: Record attachment type/date and inspect contact points for indentation, abrasion and restricted diameter growth.

lessons.title: Positioning changes light and water demand
lessons.summary: Moving leaves and shoots into stronger light changes photon exposure, leaf temperature, transpiration and the spatial pattern of demand.
lessons.cultivation: Remap the canopy after meaningful positioning changes instead of assuming the prior lighting/environment map still applies.
lessons.observe: Compare PPFD, leaf temperature, posture and irrigation response before and after repositioning.

knowledgeChecks: How can bending affect branch competition without removing tissue?

chapters.title: Topping, Pruning & Wound Recovery
chapters.objective: Differentiate tissue-removal techniques, control sanitation and evaluate wound recovery before stacking additional stress.

lessons.title: Topping changes dominance by removing an active apex
lessons.summary: Removing a shoot tip changes signaling, sink competition and future architecture while also creating a wound and removing future tissue.
lessons.cultivation: Select the cut position from the desired remaining node structure rather than a rigid universal node count.
lessons.observe: Record exact cut node, remaining buds, tool sanitation and days to resumed extension.

lessons.title: Pruning should have a defined structural purpose
lessons.summary: Leaf or branch removal can improve access, reduce unwanted density or redirect architecture, but it also removes photosynthetic area and stored resources.
lessons.cultivation: Remove only tissue linked to a stated canopy or access objective instead of treating defoliation intensity as a quality dial.
lessons.observe: Record tissue type/amount removed, canopy density, light distribution and recovery.

lessons.title: Wounding activates repair and defense signaling
lessons.summary: Cut or damaged tissue triggers wound closure, hormonal and defense responses while exposed surfaces can become infection entry points.
lessons.cultivation: Use clean tools and avoid unnecessary tissue damage when plants are already stressed or disease pressure is high.
lessons.observe: Inspect wound color, drying, cracking, softening, odor and nearby tissue over time.

lessons.title: Recovery is an acceptance step, not a calendar wait
lessons.summary: Resumed growth, stable water status, healthy wounds and restored leaf posture provide stronger release criteria than waiting a fixed number of days.
lessons.cultivation: Do not stack another severe intervention until the plant demonstrates recovery from the previous one.
lessons.observe: Track extension growth, leaf posture, irrigation response, wound condition and new symptoms.

knowledgeChecks: What biological change follows apex removal?
Why is pruning not a free redistribution of resources?
Which defense pathways respond to wounding?

chapters.title: Trellis, SCROG, Support & Mechanical Loads
chapters.objective: Use support systems to control branch position and load while preserving service access and avoiding hidden structural damage.

lessons.title: A screen is a positioning tool, not a yield guarantee
lessons.summary: SCROG or trellis systems can distribute branches across a plane, but final performance still depends on leaf area, light, roots, environment and crop timing.
lessons.cultivation: Use the screen to solve geometry and support needs rather than as an automatic production claim.
lessons.observe: Record screen height, cell size, branch locations, fill percentage and time required to manage it.

lessons.title: Support should anticipate future load
lessons.summary: Branch mass, flower mass, water on foliage, long lever arms, attachment angles and prior injuries all affect structural-failure risk.
lessons.cultivation: Install support before heavy loading makes access destructive or forces emergency ties onto brittle tissue.
lessons.observe: Track stem diameter, branch angle, unsupported span, attachment condition and load-related bending.

lessons.title: Trellis fill changes the optical target
lessons.summary: As branches occupy a screen, leaf overlap and source distance change; fixture geometry that was acceptable over an empty or sparse plane may not match the filled canopy.
lessons.cultivation: Remap PPFD after meaningful canopy fill or fixture-height changes.
lessons.observe: Preserve the same map grid, measurement plane and fixture settings for before/after comparison.

lessons.title: Serviceability is part of canopy design
lessons.summary: A dense supported canopy can obstruct irrigation service, pest scouting, sanitation, airflow inspection and safe worker access.
lessons.cultivation: Reserve paths and inspection access while the canopy is still easy to reposition.
lessons.observe: Document blocked emitters, inaccessible branches, scouting reach and time required for routine service.

chapters.title: Light Distribution, Density & Canopy Interception
chapters.objective: Evaluate canopy shape using spatial light measurements and leaf distribution rather than top-view appearance alone.

lessons.title: A canopy creates its own light gradient
lessons.summary: Upper leaves intercept photons and shade lower layers; leaf angle, overlap, branch spacing and source geometry determine how quickly light declines through the canopy.
lessons.cultivation: Architecture should be judged by the distribution of usable light, not only by how many tops are visible.
lessons.observe: Map top-plane PPFD and inspect representative interior/lower-canopy exposure.

lessons.title: Uniformity needs a declared measurement method
lessons.summary: Average PPFD can hide hotspots and dark zones, so raw grids, minima, maxima and a stated uniformity metric are more informative.
lessons.cultivation: Use the same grid and operating conditions when comparing canopy-training changes.
lessons.observe: Preserve coordinates, measurement plane, fixture state, canopy stage and raw grid values.

lessons.title: More branch tips can increase competition
lessons.summary: Increasing shoot count divides available light, root support, water and assimilate among more sinks; branch count alone does not prove better production.
lessons.cultivation: Balance tip count with available footprint, fixture distribution, root capacity and cultivar architecture.
lessons.observe: Track branch number, canopy fill, average shoot vigor, lower-canopy decline and final usable output.

lessons.title: Selective lower-canopy removal is a tradeoff
lessons.summary: Removing consistently shaded or inaccessible tissue can reduce density and labor, but excessive removal sacrifices photosynthetic surface and can add wound stress.
lessons.cultivation: Base removal on persistent location, access and measured light rather than a fixed stripping height copied from another room.
lessons.observe: Record tissue removed, local light, disease/scouting access and later branch/flower response.

chapters.title: Airflow, Microclimate & Interior Access
chapters.objective: Connect canopy density with boundary layers, humidity pockets, disease scouting and safe air movement.

lessons.title: Dense foliage creates local microclimates
lessons.summary: Leaves and flowers obstruct mixing and generate heat and water vapor, so interior temperature and humidity can differ from room averages.
lessons.cultivation: Training should preserve enough spacing to inspect and measure the interior rather than trusting one room sensor.
lessons.observe: Compare interior and exterior temperature/RH, leaf temperature and condensation risk at representative points.

lessons.title: Air movement changes boundary layers
lessons.summary: Moving air can reduce stagnant leaf boundary layers, but excessive local speed can increase water loss, abrasion and mechanical stress.
lessons.cultivation: Seek distributed circulation rather than aiming high-speed fans directly at vulnerable tissue.
lessons.observe: Check fan direction, leaf flutter, edge damage, local drying and measured environmental uniformity.

lessons.title: Circulation does not equal moisture removal
lessons.summary: Fans redistribute air while ventilation and dehumidification actually remove accumulated moisture or exchange it with another air mass.
lessons.cultivation: Do not solve a dense-canopy moisture problem only by moving the same humid air faster.
lessons.observe: Record equipment state, RH/dew-point trends and interior canopy conditions during lights-off transitions.

lessons.title: Scouting access is a biological control tool
lessons.summary: Canopy layouts that hide leaf undersides, stems, media surfaces or branch junctions delay pest, disease and mechanical-injury detection.
lessons.cultivation: Include visibility and reach in the canopy plan before the plant becomes fixed in a screen.
lessons.observe: Measure time required to inspect representative interior sites and note areas that cannot be seen or reached.

knowledgeChecks: Why can room-average RH miss canopy risk?

chapters.title: Timing, Stage, Recovery & Technique Stacking
chapters.objective: Match intervention intensity to developmental stage, plant condition and recovery capacity instead of following a universal calendar.

lessons.title: Vigor determines how much stress a plant can absorb
lessons.summary: Root health, water status, recent growth, environment, disease and previous interventions influence recovery capacity.
lessons.cultivation: Delay elective high-stress training when the plant is already managing root, water, pest, disease or environmental stress.
lessons.observe: Record recent growth rate, roots, posture, irrigation response and active symptoms before intervention.

lessons.title: Developmental stage changes the cost of restructuring
lessons.summary: Early architecture is easier to redirect, while late structural changes can remove reproductive sites, create wounds and disrupt already-established support relationships.
lessons.cultivation: Use stage-aware intervention plans instead of repeating the same training schedule on every cultivar and cycle.
lessons.observe: Record stage, days since transition, stretch status and tissue maturity at each intervention.

lessons.title: Stacked techniques destroy causal clarity
lessons.summary: Topping, pruning, transplanting, major irrigation changes and environmental changes applied together make it difficult to identify why a plant improved or declined.
lessons.cultivation: Sequence major changes when possible and define recovery before the next intervention.
lessons.observe: Keep a timestamped intervention log and compare untreated or less-treated plants where practical.

lessons.title: Recovery should be measured over time
lessons.summary: Leaf posture may recover before extension growth, wound closure or normal water use; one quick visual check is not a complete recovery assessment.
lessons.cultivation: Use multiple checkpoints before declaring the plant ready for another high-stress action.
lessons.observe: Track posture, growth, water demand, wound status and new symptoms over hours and days.

knowledgeChecks: Which plant conditions reduce training recovery capacity?

chapters.title: Measurement, Records & Outcome Review
chapters.objective: Evaluate training techniques as repeatable experiments using architecture, light, environment, labor and crop outcomes.

lessons.title: Photographs need fixed viewpoints to become data
lessons.summary: Before-and-after images are much more useful when camera position, scale, lighting and plant orientation are standardized.
lessons.cultivation: Build a repeatable canopy photo station or defined camera positions rather than relying on random attractive images.
lessons.observe: Record viewpoint, distance, plant ID, date, stage and a scale reference.

lessons.title: Architecture metrics should match the objective
lessons.summary: Height, width, branch count, node spacing, stem diameter, canopy area and support load answer different questions.
lessons.cultivation: Choose the smallest measurement set that directly tests the training goal.
lessons.observe: Define measurement points and intervals before treatment so the outcome is comparable.

lessons.title: Measure canopy performance, not just plant shape
lessons.summary: A visually even canopy can still contain poor light uniformity, hidden humid zones, inaccessible tissue or high labor cost.
lessons.cultivation: Pair architecture with light maps, environmental checks, service time and plant-health observations.
lessons.observe: Record raw map values, interior environment, scouting/service time and deviations.

lessons.title: Compare completed cycles before standardizing a method
lessons.summary: A technique becomes an SOP only after repeated crops show acceptable recovery, workflow and production outcomes under defined conditions.
lessons.cultivation: Keep cultivar and room context attached to the result instead of declaring a universal best training style.
lessons.observe: Compare labor, losses, uniformity, yield/quality endpoints and deviations across repeated cycles.
